chapter: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
title: Gladys Bentley at the Ubangi Club, formerly Connie's Inn
summary: Procope worked with Gladys Bentley at the Ubangi, describes the room and its Chinese food, and they discuss male impersonators of that era.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: What about some of the other entertainers? Do you remember -- well, Gladys Bentley, for instance?
Yes, I worked with Gladys Bentley. I
worked with Gladys Bentley down at the --
The Ubangi?
The Ubangi Club. That was after Fletcher Henderson.
What was the Ubangi like?

The Ubangi was the old Connie's Inn. It was a nice room for a nightclub, but it was built for -- I suppose it was built to be a nightclub, because it had a dance floor and bandstand and it had lights all around, you know, the floor. And they too served Chinese food.
That was very common in those days, wasn't it?
Yeah.
To have jazz in places where they had Chinese food. Were they called chop suey joints?
No. No, not these places, no. No. It was just Connie's Inn.
Uh-huh. Now Gladys, did she always wear tails and pants?
Yeah, that was her --
That was her thing.
That was her thing, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
I always found that interesting that you have -- you have female impersonators, but you don't have male impersonators today.
No.
But in those days there were several of them.
Yeah. Yeah.
She wasn't the only one, Gladys Bentley.
No. No. Oh, yeah --
There was another Gladys at that time up there. Gladys Ferguson.
I don't remember her.
Don't you?
No. There was another one. She was a singer, too. I can't remember her name, but she used to work -- she used to work around Harlem. Yeah. Gladys Bentley.
